title: Osmosis
aim: To investigate the effect of different concentrations of sucrose solution on the mass of potato cylinders, and to use the results to estimate the concentration of the solution inside the potato cells.
background: Osmosis is the diffusion of water from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane. Potato tissue is made of plant cells, each with a partially permeable cell membrane. If potato cells are placed in a solution more dilute than their cell contents, water moves into the cells by osmosis and the tissue gains mass. If the solution is more concentrated than the cell contents, water moves out and the tissue loses mass.

Potato cylinders do not all start with the same mass, so the change in mass is converted into a percentage change: percentage change = (final mass − initial mass) ÷ initial mass × 100. A gain gives a positive value and a loss gives a negative value.

When the percentage change in mass is plotted against sucrose concentration, the line of best fit crosses the x-axis (0% change) at the concentration where there is no net movement of water. At this concentration the solution outside has the same concentration as the solution inside the potato cells.
hypothesis: As the concentration of sucrose solution increases, the percentage change in mass of the potato cylinders will decrease: cylinders in dilute solutions will gain mass, and cylinders in concentrated solutions will lose mass.

variables.independent: Concentration of sucrose solution (0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1.0 mol/dm³).
variables.dependent: Percentage change in mass of the potato cylinder.
control: Same potato (same variety and age) for all cylinders
Same length and diameter of cylinder (same cork borer, cut to 3 cm), so the same surface area
Same volume of solution in each tube (10 cm³)
Same time in the solution (24 hours, or at least 30 minutes)
Cylinders blotted dry in the same way before each weighing

equipment: Six boiling tubes and a test tube rack
Sucrose solutions: 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1.0 mol/dm³, and distilled water (0.0 mol/dm³)
method: Use a cork borer to cut six potato cylinders. Push the borer into the potato on a white tile, twist and remove the cylinder. Remove any skin, as this is waterproof and would affect water movement.
Use a knife and ruler to trim all the cylinders to the same length, 3 cm, on the white tile.
Label six boiling tubes with the concentrations 0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1.0 mol/dm³ and place them in a test tube rack.
Use a measuring cylinder to add 10 cm³ of each solution to its labelled boiling tube. Rinse the measuring cylinder between solutions.
Gently blot each cylinder with a paper towel to remove surface moisture.
Weigh each cylinder on the balance and record its initial mass to 0.01 g, noting which tube it will go into.
Place one cylinder into each boiling tube and record the time. Make sure each cylinder is completely covered by the solution.
Leave the tubes in the rack at room temperature for the same length of time (for example overnight, about 24 hours).
Remove each cylinder with forceps and gently blot it dry with a paper towel in the same way as before.
Reweigh each cylinder and record its final mass.
Calculate the change in mass and the percentage change in mass for each cylinder.
Repeat the whole investigation at least twice more, then calculate the mean percentage change for each concentration.
Plot a graph of mean percentage change in mass (y-axis) against sucrose concentration (x-axis), with the y-axis including negative values. Draw a line of best fit and find where it crosses 0% change.

safety.risk: Cuts to hands when cutting and trimming the potato.
safety.precaution: Cut on a white tile, push the cork borer down into the potato, not towards your hand, and cut away from your body.

safety.risk: Slippery floor could cause a fall; sticky solution near the electronic balance.
safety.precaution: Wipe up spills straight away and keep solutions away from the balance and electrical sockets.
Keep tubes upright in a rack and report breakages to the teacher instead of picking up glass by hand.

results.notes: Percentage change = (final mass − initial mass) ÷ initial mass × 100. For 0.4 mol/dm³: (2.43 − 2.52) ÷ 2.52 × 100 = −3.6%. Plot percentage change (y-axis, with positive and negative values) against concentration (x-axis) and draw a smooth curve of best fit. It crosses 0% at about 0.3 mol/dm³.

analysis: As the sucrose concentration increases, the percentage change in mass decreases. Cylinders in distilled water and 0.2 mol/dm³ sucrose gained mass; cylinders in 0.4 mol/dm³ and above lost mass.

In distilled water and dilute solutions, the solution outside the cells is more dilute than the cell contents, so water moves into the potato cells by osmosis through their partially permeable membranes, and the cylinder gains mass. The cells become turgid, so the cylinders feel firm.

In concentrated solutions, the solution outside is more concentrated than the cell contents, so water moves out of the cells by osmosis and the cylinder loses mass. The cells become flaccid, and the cylinders feel soft and bendy.

The line of best fit crosses 0% change at about 0.3 mol/dm³. At this concentration there is no net movement of water, so the concentration of solutes inside the potato cells is equivalent to about 0.3 mol/dm³ sucrose.

The loss of mass levels off between 0.8 and 1.0 mol/dm³ (−12.0% and −12.9%). This is because the cells have already lost most of the water that can leave them, so further increases in concentration have little extra effect.

errors.error: Blotting the cylinders inconsistently leaves different amounts of surface solution, which adds to the measured mass.
errors.improvement: Blot every cylinder in exactly the same way (for example, roll once on a paper towel) before both weighings.

errors.error: Cylinders cut to slightly different lengths have different surface areas, so water moves in or out at different rates.
errors.improvement: Use the same cork borer, measure lengths carefully with a ruler, and use percentage change to allow for different starting masses.

errors.error: Water evaporates from the solutions or cylinders during the experiment, changing concentrations and masses.
errors.improvement: Cover the boiling tubes (for example with cling film or a bung) and leave them for the same length of time.

errors.error: Only one cylinder per concentration means an anomalous result has a large effect.
errors.improvement: Repeat at least three times for each concentration, identify and exclude anomalies, and calculate a mean.

examTips: Use percentage change in mass, not just change in mass, because the cylinders start with different masses. Keep the sign: a loss is negative.
To find the concentration of the potato cells, read the x-axis value where the line of best fit crosses 0% change. Explain that there is no net movement of water at that point.
Explain results using 'more dilute' and 'more concentrated' solutions and 'partially permeable membrane'. Avoid saying 'water concentration' unless you are very careful.
Remember why cylinders are blotted dry: surface solution adds mass that has not entered the cells.
When drawing the graph, your y-axis must extend below zero to show the negative values.

questions.question: Which statement best describes osmosis?
options: The movement of sucrose from a concentrated solution to a dilute solution through a partially permeable membrane
The diffusion of water from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane
The movement of water from a concentrated solution to a dilute solution using energy from respiration
The diffusion of any particle through a fully permeable membrane
markScheme: 1 mark: diffusion of water from a dilute to a concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane
questions.explanation: Osmosis is specifically about water. It moves from the dilute solution (more water) to the concentrated solution, through a partially permeable membrane, and needs no energy from respiration. Sucrose molecules are too large to cross the membrane.

questions.question:
A student placed a potato cylinder in distilled water for 24 hours.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the percentage change in mass.
markScheme: 1 mark: change in mass = 2.64 − 2.40 = 0.24 g
questions.explanation: Percentage change = change ÷ initial mass × 100. Divide by the initial mass (2.40 g), not the final mass. The answer is positive because the mass increased.

questions.question:
A student placed a potato cylinder in 0.8 mol/dm³ sucrose solution for 24 hours.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the percentage change in mass.
Include a sign in your answer.
questions.explanation: The cylinder lost mass, so the percentage change is negative: −0.32 ÷ 3.20 × 100 = −10%. Missing out the minus sign loses the information that water left the cells.

questions.question: In this investigation, why should students calculate the percentage change in mass rather than just the change in mass?
options: Percentage change is always a larger number, so it is more accurate
Percentage change removes the need to repeat the experiment
The cylinders had different starting masses, so percentage change allows a fair comparison
Percentage change shows whether sucrose entered the cells
markScheme: 1 mark: cylinders had different initial masses, so percentage change allows results to be compared
questions.explanation: A heavier cylinder would gain or lose more mass simply because it is bigger. Expressing the change as a percentage of the initial mass makes the results comparable.

questions.question: Explain why each potato cylinder is gently blotted with a paper towel before it is weighed.
acceptedAnswers: liquid on surface would add mass
only water inside cells is measured
markScheme: 1 mark: to remove solution from the surface of the cylinder
1 mark: because surface liquid would add to the mass and give an inaccurate result (it has not entered the cells)
questions.explanation: Only the water that has moved into or out of the cells should affect the mass. Liquid left on the outside adds extra mass and would make the gain look bigger or the loss look smaller.

questions.question: A potato cylinder lost mass in 1.0 mol/dm³ sucrose solution. Which explanation is correct?
options: Sucrose moved out of the potato cells into the solution
Water moved into the potato cells because the solution was more dilute
Water moved out of the potato cells by osmosis because the solution was more concentrated than the cell contents
The potato cells used up their stored starch in respiration
markScheme: 1 mark: water moved out of the cells by osmosis as the external solution was more concentrated
questions.explanation: The sucrose solution was more concentrated than the cytoplasm and cell sap, so water diffused out through the partially permeable cell membranes. Sucrose molecules are too large to cross the membrane, and respiration would cause only a tiny mass change.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows a student's results.
Assume there is a straight line between the results for 0.2 mol/dm³ and 0.4 mol/dm³.
Estimate the concentration of sucrose solution at which there would be no change in mass.
Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

headers: Concentration of sucrose solution in mol/dm³

markScheme: 1 mark: total change over 0.2 mol/dm³ is 4.0 + 3.6 = 7.6%, so 0% is 4.0 ÷ 7.6 of the way from 0.2
questions.explanation: Zero change lies between the two points. It is 4.0 ÷ 7.6 = 0.53 of the way along the 0.2 mol/dm³ gap, so the concentration is 0.2 + 0.105 = 0.31 mol/dm³. This is the concentration equivalent to the potato cell contents.

questions.explanation: These variables could all affect how much water moves in or out. Only the sucrose concentration should change, so that any difference in mass change is caused by concentration.

questions.question:
A student placed three potato cylinders in distilled water.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the mean percentage change in mass.
questions.explanation: Add the three values (33.6) and divide by the number of values (3), giving 11.2%. The values are close together, which suggests the results are repeatable.

questions.question: After 24 hours, the cylinder in distilled water felt firm and the cylinder in 1.0 mol/dm³ sucrose felt soft. What is the best explanation?
options: Cells in water became turgid; cells in concentrated sucrose became flaccid
Cells in water burst; cells in concentrated sucrose gained sucrose
Cells in water lost water; cells in concentrated sucrose gained water
Cells in water absorbed starch; cells in concentrated sucrose lost starch
markScheme: 1 mark: water cells turgid (firm), sucrose cells flaccid (soft)
questions.explanation: Water entering the cells pushes the cytoplasm against the cell wall, making them turgid and firm. Plant cells do not burst because the cell wall resists. Water leaving the cells makes them flaccid, so the tissue is soft.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows a student's results.
Suggest why the loss in mass levelled off at high concentrations of sucrose solution.

headers: Concentration of sucrose solution in mol/dm³

markScheme: 1 mark: the cells have already lost most of the water that can leave them (cells plasmolysed)
1 mark: so increasing the concentration further causes little extra water loss
questions.explanation: Once the cells have lost most of their free water, there is little more that can leave by osmosis, so the curve flattens even though the external solution becomes more concentrated.

questions.question: What is the independent variable in an investigation into the effect of sucrose concentration on the mass of potato cylinders?
options: The percentage change in mass
The length of the potato cylinders
The time left in the solution
The concentration of the sucrose solution
markScheme: 1 mark: concentration of sucrose solution
questions.explanation: The independent variable is the one deliberately changed: sucrose concentration. Percentage change in mass is the dependent variable, and cylinder length and time are control variables.

questions.question: Describe a method to find the concentration of solutes inside potato cells using potato cylinders and sucrose solutions.
markScheme: Indicative content: cut cylinders with a cork borer and trim to the same length with a knife and ruler; remove skin; prepare a range of sucrose concentrations (for example 0.0 to 1.0 mol/dm³); add the same volume of each to labelled boiling tubes; blot and weigh each cylinder on a balance; place one in each tube; leave for the same time at the same temperature; remove, blot and reweigh; calculate percentage change in mass; repeat and calculate means; plot percentage change against concentration; draw line of best fit; read concentration where line crosses 0% change, which equals the concentration of the cell contents

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent, logically ordered method including measuring mass before and after, calculating percentage change, controlling variables, and using a graph to find the concentration at 0% change.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a method with most key steps but missing either the graph or detail of control variables or percentage change.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements such as putting potato in sugar solutions and weighing, with little detail or order.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The question asks for a method that finds a concentration, so the graph and the 0% intercept are essential for the top level, as well as fair-test details such as equal lengths, equal volumes and blotting.

questions.question: Use the idea of osmosis to explain why potato cylinders gained mass in 0.2 mol/dm³ sucrose solution but lost mass in 0.6 mol/dm³ sucrose solution.
markScheme: Indicative content: potato cell contents have a solute concentration of about 0.3 mol/dm³; 0.2 mol/dm³ is more dilute than the cell contents, so water moves into the cells by osmosis; through the partially permeable cell membrane; cells gain water and mass and become turgid; 0.6 mol/dm³ is more concentrated than the cell contents, so water moves out of the cells by osmosis; cells lose mass and become flaccid; sucrose cannot cross the membrane so mass change is due to water
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explains both results by comparing each solution with the concentration of the cell contents and referring to water movement through a partially permeable membrane.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): states that water moved in or out with little or no reference to relative concentrations.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The key is comparing each external solution with the cell contents. Whether water enters or leaves depends on which side is more dilute, not just on the sucrose concentration on its own.
